entries.modern_form: Middle Persian murwārīd (Book Pahlavi mwlwʾlyt', Manichaean mwrwʾryd) 'pearl' < Old Persian *margārīta- < Proto-Iranian *mŕ̥ga-ahri-ita- 'born of the (sea-)bird's shell, oyster'
entries.note: Pahlavi murwārīd 'pearl' is real (MacKenzie 1971/1986; Nourai's -t reflects the Pahlavi spelling -yt'); gloss 'small pearl' is slightly narrow — MacKenzie simply 'pearl'. Modern scholarship (Wiktionary, Beekes s.v. μαργαρίτης, Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Greek loanwords in Middle Iranian') agrees the Iranian word is the SOURCE and Greek margaritēs the loan, so the chart's direction is right and the Borhan-e Qate' note (Persian from Greek) is rejected. One caveat: Greek margaritēs is already in Theophrastus (4th c. BCE), so the actual donor was Old Iranian *margārīta-, not Middle Persian proper; and the Aramaic/Arabic marjān branch runs through Greek (Syriac margānīṯā < Greek), not straight from Pahlavi. English margarine, Margarita and Rita do not pass through Old French.

nodes.derivation: New Persian morvārīd مروارید continues Middle Persian murwārīd (mwlwʾlyt' / mwrwʾryd) unchanged apart from vowel adjustment; Parthian morγārīd, Sogdian mrγʾrt, Khotanese mrāhe are cognates, all from Old Iranian *margārīta-, which Beekes analyses as *mŕ̥ga-ahri-ita- 'oyster', literally 'born from the shell of a (sea-)bird' (*mr̥ga- 'bird', cf. Av. mərəγa-). Attested throughout classical poetry (Hafez, 14th c., in the chart). The NOTE that Borhan-e Qate' derives it from Greek is the reverse of the modern consensus: the Greek word is the borrowing (Wiktionary; Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Greece xiii': 'most probably not borrowed from Greek margarítēs, but the borrowing may rather have functioned the other way around').

Pass-through node: the Aramaic word is Jewish Aramaic מַרְגָּנִיתָא / Syriac ܡܪܓܢܝܬܐ margānīṯā 'pearl' (with -n- for the Greek/Iranian -r-; dissimilation r…r > r…n). Wiktionary derives it from Greek μαργαρίτης, which in turn is the Iranian loan, so the ultimate source is the Iranian word as the chart says, but the immediate parent should be Greek rather than Pahlavi (a direct Iranian → Aramaic borrowing in the Achaemenid/Parthian period is not excluded but is not what the sources give).

Arabic marjān مَرْجَان 'small pearls; coral' (collective; unit noun marjāna) is borrowed from Classical Syriac margān 'pearl-like' / margānīṯā 'pearl' (Wiktionary), with Syriac g > Arabic j regularly. It is Qur'anic (55:22, 55:58 lu'lu' wa-l-marjān), where commentators already waver between 'small pearls' and 'coral' — the source of the double gloss. So the edge Aramaic → Arabic is confirmed.

Persian marjān مرجان 'coral' (also the female name Marjan) is borrowed from Arabic marjān, keeping only the 'coral' sense (Wiktionary: Persian and Ottoman Turkish 'adopted the Arabic term to mean coral specifically'); attested in Hafez alongside lu'lu' 'pearl' as in the chart's line. This is an Iranian → Greek → Aramaic → Arabic → Persian round trip, so morvārīd and marjān are doublets in Persian.

Greek μαργαρίτης (λίθος) margarítēs 'pearl' (first in Theophrastus, De lapidibus 36, 4th c. BCE; also μάργαρον) is, per Wiktionary/Beekes, a loan from Indo-Iranian, specifically the Old Iranian ancestor (*margārīta-) of Middle Persian murwārīd, with the Greek agent/material suffix -ίτης substituted for the Iranian ending; etymonline: 'from some Oriental language, most likely Iranian; cf. Middle Persian marvarit'. The edge is right in direction; only the label 'Pahlavi' for the donor is anachronistic (the loan predates Middle Persian).

Pass-through node: Latin margarīta 'pearl' (Cicero, Pliny; Vulgate Matt. 13:45–46 'pretiosa margarita'), a direct loan of Greek margarítēs with the Greek masculine -ítēs re-shaped as a Latin 1st-declension feminine -īta; Late Latin also as the female name Margarita.

Pass-through node: Old French margarite / marguerite 'pearl' and the name Margarete/Marguerite (12th–13th c.) from Latin margarīta (regular -a > -e, Latin g kept before a); Old French is the channel for English margarite, Margaret and Margery, but not for margarine, Margarita or Rita (see node 8).

nodes.words: margarite, margarine, Margaret, Marjorie, Margarita, Maggie, Rita
nodes.derivation: All seven go back to Greek margarítēs/Latin margarīta, but by different routes: margarite — Middle English 'pearl' (obsolete) from Old French margarite; the modern mineral sense (a calcium mica, 1820s) is a learned re-use with -ite. margarine — French margarine, coined by Chevreul (1813, acide margarique 'pearly acid', for the lustre of the crystals) from Greek margarítēs, then Mège-Mouriès' butter substitute (1869), English 1873: Greek → French → English, no Old French/Latin stage. Margaret — c. 1300 from Old French Margaret (Fr. Marguerite) < Late Latin Margarita. Marjorie — variant of Margery, the medieval vernacular (Old French Margerie) form of Margaret. Margarita — the Latin/Spanish form of the name (and the cocktail, from Spanish). Maggie — English pet form of Margaret; Rita — Spanish/Italian aphetic short form of Margarita/Margherita. So the chart's single Old French pass-through is right for margarite/Margaret/Marjorie/Maggie and only schematic for margarine, Margarita and Rita.

entries.modern_form: Proto-Semitic *mawt- 'death', root m-w-t 'to die' (Arabic māta, yamūtu; AHD Semitic roots mwt)
entries.note: The root is real (Proto-Semitic *mawt-; Akk. mūtu, Heb. māweṯ, Aram. mawtā, Ar. mawt) and is Common Semitic rather than specifically 'Arabic', though the Arabic reflex is what feeds Persian and Europe. The chart's two European branches diverge from modern scholarship: (a) Latin mattus 'drunk, sodden' cannot come from Arabic māt — it is attested in Petronius (1st c. CE) and is derived by Pokorny 694, de Vaan and Wiktionary from *maditus (madēre 'be wet'), PIE *meh₂d-; Nourai's own NOTE records this and modern scholarship sides with Pokorny/AHD; (b) the chess word French mat / échec et mat does come from Persian šāh māt via Arabic, but not through Latin mattus as drawn (its parent should be node 2/Arabic). Also, the māt of šāh māt is by Wiktionary's account native Persian 'stunned, at a loss', reinterpreted in Arabic as māta 'he died', so the whole Persian mât node sits awkwardly under an Arabic root. Spanish matar is of disputed origin (Latin mactāre or mattus preferred; Arabic/Persian māt is a competing minority view).

nodes.derivation: Arabic mawt مَوْت 'death' is the verbal noun (maṣdar) of the hollow verb māta / yamūtu 'to die', root m-w-t, from Proto-Semitic *mawt- (Wiktionary; cognates Akk. mūtu, Heb. māweṯ, Syr. mawtā). 'maot' is simply Nourai's rendering of mawt (aw diphthong).

mawt/mowt موت 'death' — borrowed from Arabic mawt, Iranian pronunciation mowt (Wiktionary); mamāt ممات is the Arabic maṣdar mīmī of the same verb, also borrowed: confirmed. mayyet میّت 'dead person' — Arabic mayyit, a CaCīC adjective of m-w-t (*mawīt > *mayīt > mayyit by assimilation), borrowed as a noun into Persian: confirmed. māt مات 'dead, dull; stunned, confused' — Wiktionary gives two views: Arabic māta 'he died' (the traditional one, Nourai's) or a native word connected with Sanskrit/Iranian 'measured, traversed', with the meaning 'stunned' reinforced by the chess use; unresolved. kīš-māt / šāh-māt کیش مات 'checkmate' — Wiktionary analyses šāh-māt as Persian 'the king is stunned/helpless', with Arabic speakers re-etymologising māt as 'died' before the phrase reached Europe; Barnhart and etymonline give the same alternative. So the Arabic derivation of māt/šāh-māt is the classical account but not the only modern one; node verdict follows the weakest word.

Latin mattus (also mātus) 'drunk, maudlin; sodden, dull' is attested in Petronius (Satyricon 41, 1st c. CE) — six centuries before any Arabic contact — so it cannot derive from Arabic/Persian māt. The standard etymology (Pokorny IEW 694 s.v. mad-, de Vaan, Wiktionary) is *maditus 'wetted' (past participle of madēre 'to be wet, be drunk', PIE *meh₂d-, cf. Skt. mattá- 'drunk') with syncope and assimilation -dt- > -tt-. Nourai's own NOTE ('POK:694 derives mattus from Mad: wet') records the correct view; modern scholarship is unanimous on Pokorny's side, and Nourai's FSD (Funk & Wagnalls) source is superseded. The parent edge Persian māt → Latin mattus is therefore rejected.

French mat 'matte, dull, without lustre' continues Old French mat 'beaten down, withered, dejected; dull' (12th c.), which Wiktionary and TLF derive from Latin mattus 'sodden, dull' — so the edge Latin mattus → French mat is the majority view and is right as drawn; etymonline adds the alternative that the Old French adjective is a transferred use of chess mat 'checkmated' (from Arabic šāh māt), in which case this word would after all descend from node 2 (but not through Latin). Either way it does not go back to Arabic through Latin.

English mat/matte 'dull, lustreless' (1640s) is borrowed from French mat; the spelling matte was not standardised until the 20th c. AHD:805 (the chart's NOTE) refers it to the IE root mad- 'wet' via Latin mattus — which, as with node 3, is the modern consensus; the French → English edge itself is uncontroversial.

Old French mat 'checkmated, defeated' (12th c.; verb mater 'to checkmate, overcome') and the phrase eschec mat > Modern French échec et mat are the chess term, from Arabic šāh māt (Persian šāh māt 'the king is stunned/helpless', re-read in Arabic as 'the king is dead'), which reached the Romance languages with chess itself through Muslim Spain and Sicily in the 10th–11th c. (Spanish jaque mate, Italian scacco matto, Medieval Latin scaccum mattum). The chart draws this French mat from Latin mattus 'drunk' — that edge is wrong: the checkmate word is an Arabic/Persian loan and should hang directly from node 2 (Persian/Arabic māt), as Nourai's own NOTE ('debatable paths') half-concedes. Its ultimate Semitic vs. Persian identity is the open question discussed at node 2.

English mate (v.2) 'to checkmate; to overcome, confound' (c. 1300) from Old French mater 'to checkmate, defeat' (< mat); mate (n.2) 'checkmate' likewise c. 1300 from Old French mat; checkmate (mid-14th c.) from Old French eschec mat, ultimately Arabic šāh māt. The figurative 'to thwart' sense is late-14th-c. AHD Semitic roots mwt lists exactly these two English derivatives.

Spanish matar 'to kill' (also Portuguese, Catalan) is of disputed origin. Wiktionary: 'most likely from Latin mactāre (through a Vulgar Latin *mattāre)', alternatively from Late Latin mattus 'drunk, stupefied' (*mattāre 'to stun'), or influenced by Arabic māta 'to die'; RAE likewise prefers Vulgar Latin *mattare < mattus. Etymonline notes the phonological difficulty of mactāre (expected *mechar) and gives Arabic māta (borrowed from Persian māt) as the alternative — the view Klein (KLN:946, Nourai's source) adopts and Corominas discusses via the chess word. So the Arabic derivation is a real scholarly option but not the preferred one. matador 'killer; the bullfighter who kills the bull' is transparently matar + agent suffix -dor (Latin -tōrem): confirmed as a derivative.
French matador is borrowed from Spanish matador in the late 17th–18th c. with the bullfighting vocabulary (Wiktionary: 'Borrowed from Spanish matador'); form unchanged.

Persian mātādor ماتادور (the chart's spelling ماتادُر marks the short o) is a 20th-c. loan; Wiktionary labels it 'borrowed from Spanish matador', whereas Nourai (following Mo'in, MON:3678) routes it through French, which was the usual channel for European words into Persian in that period and is phonetically indistinguishable here. Both routes are compatible; the immediate donor cannot be decided from the form.
English matador (1670s) is borrowed directly from Spanish matador 'killer', agent noun of matar; also used from 1730s for the top trump cards in ombre/quadrille (Spanish card games).
